HSBC Holdings plc Earnings Release 3Q26
27 October 2026
 
 
Georges Elhedery, Group CEO, said:
 
“Our performance shows that in a more complex world clients continue to turn to us to navigate uncertainty and seize new opportunities. It also reflects consistent execution of our strategic priorities with pace, precision and discipline. As we simplify HSBC, we are creating greater capacity to invest, grow and deliver strong returns for our shareholders.”
 
 
Financial performance in 3Q26
 
-
Profit before tax increased by $2.3bn or 32% to $9.6bn compared with 3Q25, primarily due to a net favourable impact from notable items of $1.4bn, which reflected the non-recurrence of legal provisions in 3Q25 of $1.4bn. The increase also reflected growth in revenue, mainly from banking net interest income (‘banking NII’) and lower expected credit losses and other credit impairment charges (‘ECL’). Profit after tax increased by $2.1bn or 38% to $7.6bn compared with 3Q25.
-
Constant currency profit before tax excluding notable items increased by $0.9bn to $10.0bn compared with 3Q25.
-
Annualised return on average tangible equity (‘RoTE‘) in 3Q26 was 17.7% compared with 12.3% in 3Q25. Excluding notable items, annualised RoTE in 3Q26 was 18.2%, a rise of 1.6 percentage points compared with 3Q25.
-
Revenue increased by $0.8bn to $18.6bn compared with 3Q25, primarily reflecting growth in banking NII. Fee and other income also increased in our Corporate and Institutional Banking (‘CIB’) business in Wholesale Transaction Banking (‘WTB’) and in Debt and Equity Markets, supported by higher customer activity, and in Investment Distribution and Private Bank in Wealth. This was partly offset by valuation losses in Corporate Centre and the non-recurrence of one-off favourable impacts in 3Q25 in Insurance. Constant currency revenue excluding notable items rose by $0.8bn to $18.7bn.
-
Net interest income (‘NII’) of $9.3bn increased by $0.5bn or 6% compared with 3Q25. The increase reflected deposit balance growth and the benefit of reinvestment of our structural hedge at higher yields, partly offset by lower NII from Markets Treasury and an adverse impact of $0.1bn from one-off items in 3Q26. Banking NII increased by $0.6bn to $11.7bn. Banking NII excludes insurance NII, which fell by $0.1bn, and the funding costs associated with the trading book, which remained broadly stable.
-
Net interest margin (‘NIM’) of 1.57% was stable compared with 3Q25.
-
ECL of $0.8bn decreased by $0.2bn or 17% compared with 3Q25, primarily reflecting a $0.1bn reduction in stage 3 charges related to the Hong Kong commercial real estate (‘CRE’) sector, as well as lower charges in our UK business and International Wealth and Premier Banking (‘IWPB’) business in Mexico.
-
Operating expenses of $8.8bn were $1.3bn or 12% lower compared with 3Q25. This included a favourable net impact of $1.4bn from notable items, which reflected the non-recurrence of legal provisions in 3Q25. Excluding notable items, the increase in operating expenses primarily reflected the impact of inflation, higher planned spend and investment in technology, and the phasing of the performance-related pay accrual relative to 3Q25, partly mitigated by the cost reduction benefits from our organisational simplification. Target basis operating expenses were $0.1bn or 1.4% higher than in 3Q25, including the impact of inflation and higher planned spend and investment in technology, partly offset by the cost reduction benefits from our organisational simplification.
-
Customer lending balances increased by $7.8bn compared with 2Q26 on a reported basis. On a constant currency basis, lending balances increased by $6.7bn. This primarily reflected growth as we supported our customers to participate in the India Foreign Currency Non-Resident Deposit scheme, together with growth in our UK and Hong Kong businesses. This was partly offset by the classification to held for sale of lending balances associated with the exit of our retail banking business in Australia in our IWPB business.
-
Customer accounts increased by $9.1bn compared with 2Q26 on a reported basis. On a constant currency basis, customer accounts increased by $6.5bn, reflecting continued momentum in deposit inflows in our Hong Kong business. In our IWPB business, deposit growth was mainly in India, as we facilitated customer participation in the India Foreign Currency Non-Resident Deposit scheme. This growth was partly offset by retail deposit outflows following our announced exit of our retail banking business in Australia. In CIB, lower deposit balances reflected outflows of short-term balances.
-
Common equity tier 1 (‘CET1’) capital ratio of 13.9% decreased by 0.2 percentage points compared with 30 June 2026, reflecting an increase in risk-weighted assets (‘RWAs‘), together with a decrease in the fair value of hold-to-collect-and-sell debt instruments due to higher yields and the impact of the share buy-back announced at our interim results, partly offset by regulatory profits net of dividends.
-
The Board has approved a third interim dividend of $0.10 per share. On 28 September 2026, we completed the $1bn share buy-back announced at our interim results. We also intend to initiate a share buy-back of up to $1bn, which we expect to complete by our 2026 full-year results announcement.
 
 
Financial performance in 9M26
 
-
Profit before tax increased by $6.0bn or 26% to $29.2bn compared with 9M25. The increase primarily reflected a net favourable impact of $3.7bn from notable items. The increase also reflected revenue growth from an increase in banking NII and higher fee and other income, primarily in Wealth and WTB. Profit after tax of $22.9bn was $4.9bn or 28% higher compared with 9M25.
-
The net favourable movement in notable items primarily reflected the non-recurrence of 9M25 dilution and impairment losses of $2.1bn related to our associate Bank of Communications Co., Limited (‘BoCom’) and legal provisions of $1.4bn, together with lower restructuring costs associated with our organisational simplification of $0.3bn. These items were partly offset by disposal losses recognised on the classification to held for sale associated with the planned sale of our business in Malta of $0.3bn in 9M26.
-
Constant currency profit before tax excluding notable items increased by $2.0bn to $30.4bn compared with 9M25.
-
Annualised RoTE in 9M26 was 18.0%. Excluding notable items, annualised RoTE in 9M26 was 18.8%, a rise of 1.1 percentage points compared with 9M25.
 
-
Revenue increased by $4.5bn or 9% to $56.4bn compared with 9M25, including a net favourable impact from notable items of $0.9bn and a favourable impact from foreign currency translation differences of $0.7bn. The remaining increase reflected higher banking NII, and fee and other income growth in Wealth across our IWPB and Hong Kong businesses, supported by higher customer activity, and in WTB, mainly in our CIB business. Constant currency revenue excluding notable items rose by $2.8bn to $56.8bn compared with 9M25.
-
NII increased by $1.9bn compared with 9M25, primarily driven by deposit balance growth, the benefit of reinvestment of our structural hedge at higher yields, and the favourable impact of foreign currency translation differences of $0.4bn. This was partly offset by lower NII from Markets Treasury. Banking NII increased by $2.2bn to $34.6bn, as the deduction for insurance NII reduced by $0.2bn, due to the impact of strategic transactions. The funding costs associated with the trading book, which are also excluded from banking NII, rose by $0.1bn.
-
NIM of 1.60% was 3 basis points (‘bps‘) higher compared with 9M25, mainly due to the impact from foreign currency translation differences and the benefit of our structural hedge, partly offset by lower market interest rates.

ECL of $3.2bn were $0.2bn higher than in 9M25. The 9M26 charge primarily reflected stage 3 charges on wholesale exposures, including a $0.5bn fraud-related, secondary, securitisation exposure with a financial sponsor in the UK in our CIB business. The 9M26 charge also included $0.3bn related to the Hong Kong CRE sector and allowances to reflect uncertainty due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. ECL in 9M25 included charges of $0.7bn related to the Hong Kong CRE sector and a charge against a Middle Eastern exposure.
-
Operating expenses of $26.2bn were $0.9bn or 3% lower than in 9M25, including a favourable net impact of $1.8bn from notable items, which comprised the non-recurrence of legal provisions in 9M25 of $1.4bn and lower restructuring and other related costs associated with our organisational simplification of $0.3bn. Excluding notable items, the increase in expenses primarily reflected an adverse impact of $0.4bn from foreign currency translation differences, higher planned spend and investment in technology and Wealth, and the impact of inflation, partly mitigated by cost reductions from our organisational simplification. Target basis operating expenses were $0.5bn or 2.0% higher than in 9M25, including higher planned spend and investment in technology and the impact of inflation, partly offset by cost reductions from our organisational simplification.
-
 
 
Outlook
 
Group financial targets
-
We remain confident in achieving the targets we set out in February 2026, including a RoTE of 17% or better for 2026, 2027 and 2028, excluding notable items.
-
We continue to target year-on-year growth in revenue from 2026 to 2028, rising to 5% growth in 2028 compared with 2027, excluding notable items and on a constant currency basis.
-
We maintain our dividend payout ratio target basis of 50% for 2026, 2027 and 2028. Our target basis payout ratio is calculated as a percentage of earnings per share, excluding material notable items and related impacts.
In respect of 2026
-
We continue to expect banking NII of at least $46bn in 2026.
-
We continue to expect an ECL charge as a percentage of average gross customer loans of around 45bps (including held for sale loan balances) for 2026. Over the medium term, we retain our planning range of 30–40bps.
-
The Group remains on track to deliver year-on-year growth in operating expenses of approximately 1% in 2026 on a target basis. As communicated at our 2026 interim results, should strong business performance continue, we may consider additional performance-related pay, which would increase 2026 target basis cost growth modestly. Our target basis operating expenses measure excludes notable items and includes the impact of simplification-related saves associated with our announced strategic reorganisation.
Capital and regulatory developments
-
We continue to assess the anticipated impact of the final Basel 3.1 standards on our capital. We expect, based on our latest modelling, that the impact on the Group CET1 capital ratio at 1 January 2027 will be a benefit of approximately 40–50bps. The final impact will depend on a number of factors, including model and data refinements, portfolio size and composition and supervisory permissions granted. Any related reductions to firm-specific capital requirements are not expected to be significant.
-
We intend to continue to manage our CET1 capital ratio within our medium-term target operating range of 14% to 14.5%.
Ñ   Our targets and expectations reflect our current outlook for the global macroeconomic environment and market-dependent factors, such as market-implied interest rates (as of mid-October 2026) and rates of foreign exchange, as well as customer behaviour and activity levels.
Ñ  We do not reconcile our forward guidance on RoTE excluding notable items, target basis operating expenses, dividend payout ratio target basis or banking NII to their equivalent reported measures.

About HSBC
 
HSBC Holdings plc, the parent company of HSBC, is headquartered in London. With assets of $3.4tn at 30 September 2026, HSBC is one of the world’s largest banking and financial services organisations.
 
The Group‘s operating segments comprise of four businesses along with Corporate Centre:
 
-
Hong Kong
-
UK
-
Corporate and Institutional Banking
-
International Wealth and Premier Banking
 
Our Hong Kong business comprises Retail Banking and Wealth and Commercial Banking of HSBC Hong Kong and Hang Seng Bank Limited (‘Hang Seng Bank‘). Our UK business comprises UK Retail Banking and Wealth (including first direct and M&S Bank) and UK Commercial Banking, including HSBC Innovation Bank. CIB integrates our Commercial Banking business (outside of the UK and Hong Kong) with our Global Banking and Markets business. IWPB comprises Premier banking outside of Hong Kong and the UK, our Private Bank, Asset Management and Insurance businesses. Corporate Centre results primarily comprise the financial impact from certain acquisitions and disposals and the share of profit, dilution and impairment loss impacts from interests in our associates and joint ventures. It also includes Central Treasury, stewardship costs and consolidation adjustments.

Reshaping the Group for growth
 
Privatisation of Hang Seng Bank
On 26 January 2026, we completed our privatisation of Hang Seng Bank, following shareholder and Court approval. Hang Seng Bank is now a wholly-owned subsidiary of the HSBC Group and Hang Seng Bank shares have been withdrawn from the Hong Kong Stock Exchange. Through the privatisation of Hang Seng Bank, we expect to realise $0.5bn in annualised pre-tax revenue and cost synergies across both our brands in Hong Kong by the end of 2028. We expect to incur associated restructuring costs of $0.6bn, of which one-off income statement impacts would be reported as material notable items. We also have an ambition to generate further annualised revenue and cost opportunities of around $0.4bn by the end of 2028 across both our brands in Hong Kong.
 
Organisational simplification
At our 2024 full-year results we announced measures to simplify the Group, committing to deliver an annualised reduction of around $1.5bn in our cost base by the end of 2026, spending $1.8bn in restructuring and other related costs. At our 1H26 interim results, having already exceeded our savings commitment of $1.5bn, we revised our simplification savings commitment with an intention to action around $2bn of annualised savings by the end of 2026, spending up to our originally expected $1.8bn of restructuring costs. The additional saves we have brought into the programme generate capacity that will be used to support the growth of our four businesses.
 
Since the start of 2025, we have identified and actioned annualised cost savings of approximately $1.9bn, spending associated restructuring and other related costs of $1.6bn. These actions have resulted in a reduction of around $0.6bn in operating expenses in the income statement in 2025, and a $0.8bn reduction in 9M26.
 
Strategic transactions
We remain focused on opportunities where we have a clear competitive advantage and accretive returns, and we aim to redeploy approximately $1.8bn of additional costs saved from non-strategic activities into these areas over the medium term. This includes the additional $0.3bn of costs saved from the synergies generated from our privatisation of Hang Seng Bank.
 
During the third quarter of 2026, we completed the sale of our operations in Uruguay. In addition, we announced the sale of HSBC Life Singapore. In Australia, we announced the sale of our portfolio of home and personal loans, the planned wind-down of the remaining retail business and the transfer of our CIB, Private Banking and Asset Management businesses to the Sydney branch of The Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation Limited, simplifying our entity footprint. In Egypt, we announced the sale of our retail banking business. The completion of announced disposals and related actions remains subject to relevant regulatory and other approvals. We have commenced a strategic review of our retail business and domestic-focused small and mid-sized corporate banking operations in Türkiye. Our international wholesale client business in Türkiye is unaffected by this review.
 
Ñ
For further details on business disposals, see page 13.
 
Progress in growth areas
Wealth balances increased by 3% to $1.6tn at 30 September 2026 compared with 31 December 2025. We attracted net new money (‘NNM‘) in 9M26 of $105bn, with $95bn booked in Asia, partly offset by the impact of classifications to held for sale and portfolio exits.
 
Transaction banking continues to perform well as we leverage our network and capabilities to capture opportunities from changing trade and capital flows. In 9M26, fee and other income in WTB rose by 8% compared with 9M25, or by 6% on a constant currency basis, reflecting increases in Global Foreign Exchange, Securities Services, Global Trade Solutions (‘GTS‘) and Global Payment Solutions (‘GPS‘).

Basis of presentation
 
Constant currency performance
Constant currency performance is computed by adjusting reported results for the effects of foreign currency translation differences, which reflect the movements of the US dollar against most major currencies during 2026. Excluding these differences allows us to assess balance sheet and income statement performance on a like-for-like basis and to better understand the underlying trends in the business. Foreign currency translation differences at 30 September 2026 are computed by retranslating into US dollars for non-US dollar branches, subsidiaries, joint ventures and associates:
 
-
the income statements for 9M25 at the average rate of exchange for 9M26;
-
the income statements for the quarterly periods at the average rate of exchange for 3Q26;
-
the closing prior period balance sheets at the prevailing rates of exchange on 30 September 2026.
 
No adjustment has been made to the exchange rates used to translate foreign currency-denominated assets and liabilities into the functional currencies of any HSBC branches, subsidiaries, joint ventures or associates. The constant currency data of our operations in Türkiye has not been adjusted further for the impacts of hyperinflation. When reference is made to foreign currency translation differences in tables or commentaries, comparative data reported in the functional currencies of HSBC’s operations has been translated at the appropriate exchange rates applied in the current period on the basis described above.
 
Notable items and material notable items
We separately disclose ‘notable items’, which are components of our income statement that management would consider as outside the normal course of business and generally non-recurring in nature.
 
Certain notable items are classified as ‘material notable items’, which are a subset of notable items. Categorisation as a material notable item is dependent on the nature of each item in conjunction with the financial impact on the Group‘s income statement, and such items are excluded from our target basis dividend payout ratio calculation and earnings per share measure. Material notable items in 9M26 or relevant comparative periods relate to the operating expenses associated with actions to exit or wind down non-strategic businesses. They also include a dilution loss and the recognition of an impairment of our investment in BoCom in 9M25, and a legal provision relating to developments in a claim in Luxembourg relating to the Bernard L. Madoff Investment Securities LLC fraud in 9M25.
 
Ñ
The tables on pages 25 to 29 and pages 32 to 36 detail the effects of notable items on each of our business segments and legal entities.
 
Impact of strategic transactions
In addition to the items categorised as material notable items, the impacts of strategic transactions include the distorting impact observed between the periods of the operating income statement results related to acquisitions, disposals and wind-downs that affect period-on-period comparisons. Once a transaction has completed or a wind-down has commenced, the impact will include the operating income statement results of each business, which are not classified as notable items, in any comparative period if there are no results in the current period as a result of a transaction, or a reduction in revenue or costs has arisen from the wind-down of a business. We consider the monthly impact of distorting income statement results when calculating the impact of strategic transactions. In the case of wind-downs, or transactions that complete in phased tranches, there may be timing differences between the recognition of operating cost impacts and operating revenue impacts. These would arise in the event that there is a timing lag between the impact of cost actions and the resultant impact on operating revenue.
 
Ñ
See page 30 for further details on the impact of strategic transactions.
 
Management view of revenue on a constant currency basis
We provide breakdowns of revenue for each of our business segments on a constant currency basis by major product. These reflect the basis on which revenue performance of the businesses is assessed and managed. In the management view of revenue, notable items are presented separately.
 
We group certain products in a consistent manner across our business segments. WTB comprises our Global Foreign Exchange, GPS, GTS and Securities Services businesses. Wealth comprises our Investment Distribution, Insurance, Private Bank and Asset Management businesses.
 
On page 7 we provide a summarised management view of revenue for the Group‘s results, on reported foreign exchange rates, to supplement the Group‘s reported revenue performance using the product grouping which is used to manage and assess our segmental performance.
 
Impact of hyperinflationary accounting
We continue to treat Türkiye as a hyperinflationary economy for accounting purposes. The impact of applying International Accounting Standard (‘IAS’) 29 ‘Financial Reporting in Hyperinflationary Economies’ and the hyperinflation provisions of IAS 21 ’The Effects of Changes in Foreign Exchange Rates’ in the current period on our operations in Türkiye was a decrease in the Group’s profit before tax of $146m for 9M26 and a decrease of $40m for 3Q26 (9M25: $119m decrease; 2Q26: $44m decrease; 3Q25: $40m decrease). The consumer price index at 30 September 2026 for Türkiye was 137.23 (30 June 2026: 129.99; 30 September 2025: 105.78).
 
 
Use of alternative performance measures
 
Our reported results are prepared in accordance with International Financial Reporting Standards as issued by the International Accounting Standards Board (‘IFRS Accounting Standards‘), as detailed in our financial statements starting on page 262 of the Annual Report and Accounts 2025.
 
To measure our performance, we supplement our IFRS Accounting Standards figures with non-IFRS Accounting Standards measures, which constitute alternative performance measures under European Securities and Markets Authority guidance and non-GAAP financial measures defined in and presented in accordance with the US Securities and Exchange Commission rules and regulations. These measures include those derived from our reported results that eliminate factors distorting period-on-period comparisons. The ‘constant currency performance’ measure used throughout this report is described on page 5. Definitions and calculations of other alternative performance measures are included in ‘Alternative performance measures’ on page 37. All alternative performance measures are reconciled to the closest reported performance measure.
 
Return on average tangible equity excluding notable items
The calculation for RoTE excluding notable items adjusts the ‘profit attributable to the ordinary shareholders, excluding goodwill and other intangible assets impairment‘ for the post-tax impact of notable items. To better align with market practice, from our 2025 full-year results, we no longer adjust the ‘average tangible equity‘ for the post-tax impact of notable items in each period. Comparatives have been re-presented.
 
Ñ
See page 37 for the definition of return on average tangible equity excluding notable items and page 38 for the reconciliation to the GAAP measure.
 
Banking net interest income
Banking net interest income (‘banking NII‘) adjusts our NII primarily for the impact of funding trading and fair value activities reported in interest expense. It represents the Group’s banking revenue that is directly impacted by changes in interest rates. We use this measure to determine the deployment of our surplus funding and to help optimise our structural hedging and risk management actions.
 
Ñ
For more information on banking NII, including the reconciliation to the GAAP measure, see page 11.
 
Constant currency revenue and profit before tax excluding notable items and the impact of strategic transactions
To aid the understanding of our results, we separately report ‘constant currency revenue excluding notable items‘ and ‘constant currency profit before tax excluding notable items‘, which exclude the impact of notable items and the impact of foreign exchange translation. We also separately disclose ‘constant currency revenue excluding notable items and the impact of strategic transactions‘ and ‘constant currency profit before tax excluding notable items and the impact of strategic transactions‘, which also exclude the impact of strategic transactions classified as material notable items. We consider these measures to provide useful information to investors as they remove items that distort period-on-period comparisons.
The impact of strategic transactions also includes the distorting impact between the periods of the operating income statement results related to acquisitions and disposals and that affect period-on-period comparisons. These impacts are not included in our notable or material notable items. The impact of strategic transactions is computed by including the operating income statement results of each business in any period for which there are no results in the comparative period.
 
Ñ
See page 38 for the reconciliation to the GAAP measure.
 
Target basis operating expenses
Target basis operating expenses include the impact of simplification-related saves associated with our announced strategic reorganisation, is measured on a constant currency basis and excludes notable items and the impact of retranslating the prior year results of hyperinflationary economies at constant currency, which we consider to be outside of our control. We consider target basis operating expenses to provide useful information to investors by quantifying and excluding the notable items that management considered when setting and assessing cost-related targets.
Ñ
See page 40 for the reconciliation to the GAAP measure.
 
Basic earnings per share excluding material notable items and related impacts
We have established a dividend payout ratio target basis of 50% for 2026. For the purposes of computing our dividend payout ratio target basis, we exclude from earnings per share material notable items and related impacts.
Related impacts include those items that do not qualify for designation as notable items but whose adjustment is considered by management to be appropriate for the purposes of determining the basis for our dividend payout ratio target basis calculation, which we exclude from earnings per share material notable items and related impacts.
Ñ
See page 30 for the supplementary analysis of the impact of strategic transactions.
Ñ
See page 37 for the definition of ‘basic earnings per share excluding material notable items and related impacts‘ and page 40 for the reconciliation to the GAAP measure.

3Q26 compared with 3Q25 – performance commentary  
 
Reported profit before tax of $9.6bn was $2.3bn or 32% higher than in 3Q25, primarily reflecting a net favourable impact from notable items, primarily due to the non-recurrence of legal provisions of $1.4bn in 3Q25. The increase also reflected growth in revenue, mainly from banking NII, and lower ECL.
On a constant currency basis, profit before tax was $2.3bn higher than in 3Q25. On the same basis and excluding notable items, profit before tax was $0.9bn higher than in 3Q25.
Reported revenue increased by $0.8bn or 5% to $18.6bn, primarily reflecting growth in banking NII. Fee and other income also rose in CIB in WTB across all products, supported by higher customer activity, as well as in Debt and Equity Markets, mainly in Prime Finance. Fee and other income also increased in Investment Distribution and Private Bank in Wealth from increased client activity, partly offset by valuation losses in Corporate Centre, the non-recurrence of 3Q25 one-off favourable impacts and an adverse impact from strategic transactions in Insurance.
NII increased by $0.5bn compared with 3Q25. The increase reflected deposit growth and the benefit of reinvestment of our structural hedge at higher yields, partly offset by lower NII from Markets Treasury and an adverse impact of $0.1bn from one-off items in 3Q26. Banking NII increased by $0.6bn to $11.7bn. Banking NII excludes insurance NII, which fell by $0.1bn, and the funding costs associated with the trading book, which remained broadly stable. Banking NII increased by $0.6bn on a constant currency basis.
Reported ECL in 3Q26 of $0.8bn were $0.2bn lower compared with 3Q25, primarily reflecting a $0.1bn reduction in stage 3 charges related to the Hong Kong CRE sector, as well as lower charges in our UK business and in our IWPB business in Mexico.
←  
For further details of the calculation of ECL, including the measurement uncertainties and significant judgements applied to such calculations, the impact of the economic scenarios and management judgemental adjustments, see pages 45 to 50.
  
Reported operating expenses of $8.8bn were $1.3bn or 12% lower than in 3Q25. This included a favourable net impact of $1.4bn from notable items, which primarily reflected the non-recurrence of legal provisions in 3Q25 of $1.4bn. Excluding notable items, the increase in operating expenses primarily reflected the impact of inflation, higher planned spend and investment in technology, and the phasing of the performance-related pay accrual relative to 3Q25, partly mitigated by the cost reduction benefits from our organisational simplification. Target basis operating expenses were $0.1bn or 1.4% higher than in 3Q25, primarily due to the impact of inflation and higher planned spend and investment in technology, partly offset by the cost reduction benefits from our organisational simplification.
Reported share of profit from associates and joint ventures less impairment of $0.7bn was $0.1bn or 13% higher compared with 3Q25, reflecting increases from Saudi Awwal Bank (‘SAB‘) and BoCom.
Tax expense in 3Q26 was a charge of $2.1bn, representing an effective tax rate of 21.4%. Tax expense in 3Q25 was a charge of $1.8bn, representing an effective tax rate of 24.6%. The effective tax rate for 3Q25 was increased by 4.4% due to legal provisions on which no tax benefit was recorded.
Dividend
On 27 October 2026, the Board announced a third interim dividend for 2026 of $0.10 per ordinary share. For further details, see page 54.

9M26 compared with 9M25 – performance commentary
Reported profit before tax of $29.2bn was $6.0bn higher than in 9M25, primarily reflecting a $3.7bn net favourable impact from notable items together with revenue growth from an increase in banking NII and higher fee and other income, primarily in Wealth and WTB.
 
The net favourable movement in notable items primarily reflected the non-recurrence of 9M25 dilution and impairment losses of $2.1bn related to our associate BoCom and legal provisions of $1.4bn, together with lower restructuring costs associated with our organisational simplification of $0.3bn. These items were partly offset by disposal losses recognised on the classification to held for sale associated with the planned sale of our business in Malta of $0.3bn in 9M26.
 
On a constant currency basis, profit before tax of $29.2bn was $5.9bn higher than in 9M25. On the same basis and excluding notable items, profit before tax of $30.4bn was $2.0bn or 7% higher compared with 9M25.
 
Reported revenue of $56.4bn was $4.5bn or 9% higher than in 9M25 including a $0.9bn net favourable impact from notable items, which primarily related to the non-recurrence of a dilution loss of $1.1bn on BoCom recognised in 9M25, partly offset by higher net losses from business disposals.
 
Revenue excluding notable items increased by $3.6bn or 7%, reflecting higher banking NII, and growth in fee and other income. The fee and other income growth reflected a strong performance in Wealth, driven by increases in Investment Distribution in both our IWPB and Hong Kong businesses, and in Private Bank supported by higher customer activity. In addition, there was growth in Insurance fee and other income, driven primarily by a higher contractual service margin (‘CSM’) release as a result of strong new business growth in Hong Kong.
 
Fee and other income also increased in our CIB business. This was mainly in WTB, reflecting growth across all products, supported by higher customer activity, and also in Debt and Equity Markets, partly offset by a reduction in Investment Banking fee and other income due to the wind-down of our Mergers and Acquisitions (‘M&A’) and Equity Capital Markets (‘ECM’) businesses in the UK, Europe and the US.
 
In Corporate Centre, fee and other income was lower, primarily driven by valuation losses on financial instruments and structural foreign exchange hedges, together with the non-recurrence of fair value gains on non-qualifying hedges related to our retained French portfolio of home and certain other loans. This was partly offset by a one-off $0.2bn gain from a property asset disposal in 9M26.
 
NII increased by $1.9bn compared with 9M25, primarily driven by deposit balance growth and the benefit of reinvestment of our structural hedge at higher yields, and the favourable impact of foreign currency translation differences of $0.4bn. This was partly offset by lower NII from Markets Treasury. Banking NII increased by $2.2bn to $34.6bn, as the deduction for insurance NII reduced by $0.2bn due to the impact of strategic transactions. The funding costs associated with generating trading and fair value income were $7.2bn, an increase of $0.1bn compared with 9M25, as the impact of higher trading balances was partly offset by lower market interest rates.
 
Reported ECL charge of $3.2bn was $0.2bn or 8% higher than in 9M25. The charge in 9M26 primarily reflected stage 3 charges on wholesale exposures, including a $0.5bn fraud-related, secondary, securitisation exposure with a financial sponsor in the UK in our CIB business. The 9M26 charge also included $0.3bn related to the Hong Kong CRE sector and allowances to reflect uncertainty due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. ECL in 9M25 included charges related to the Hong Kong CRE sector of $0.7bn, as well as allowance increases relating to geopolitical tensions and higher trade tariffs.
 
Reported operating expenses of $26.2bn were $0.9bn or 3% lower than in 9M25, reflecting a favourable net impact of $1.8bn from notable items, which comprised the non-recurrence of legal provisions in 9M25 of $1.4bn and lower restructuring and other related costs associated with our organisational simplification of $0.3bn. Excluding notable items, the increase in expenses primarily reflected an adverse impact of $0.4bn from foreign currency translation differences, higher planned spend and investment in technology and Wealth, the impact of inflation, the phasing of the performance-related pay accrual relative to 9M25 and other cost growth. These increases were partly mitigated by cost reductions from our organisational simplification. Target basis operating expenses were $0.5bn or 2% higher than in 9M25 reflecting higher planned spend and investment in technology, and the impacts of inflation, partly offset by cost reductions from our organisational simplification.
The number of employees expressed in full-time equivalent staff at 30 September 2026 was 204,330, a decrease of 4,390 from 31 December 2025. The number of contractors at 30 September 2026 was 4,087, an increase of 113 from 31 December 2025.
 
Reported share of profit from associates and joint ventures of $2.2bn increased by $1.0bn, mainly due to the non-recurrence of an impairment loss of $1.0bn recognised on BoCom in 9M25.
 
Tax expense in 9M26 was a charge of $6.3bn, representing an effective tax rate of 21.5% (9M25: 22.3%). The effective tax rate for 9M26 was increased by the non-deductible losses recorded on the sales of HSBC Life (UK) Limited and our business in Uruguay, and the planned sale of our business in Malta. Excluding these items, the effective tax rate for 9M26 was 21.1%. Tax expense in 9M25 was a charge of $5.2bn, representing an effective tax rate of 22.3%, increased by the non-deductible impairment and dilution loss in BoCom and legal provisions on which no tax benefit is recorded. Excluding these items, the effective tax rate for 9M25 was 19.9%.

2 Net interest spread is the difference between the average annualised interest rate earned on AIEA, net of amortised premiums and loan fees, and the average annualised interest rate payable on average interest-bearing funds.

NII in 3Q26 of $9.3bn was $0.5bn higher compared with 3Q25. This mainly reflected deposit growth and the benefit of reinvestment of our structural hedge at higher yields, partly offset by lower NII from Markets Treasury and the impact of an adverse $0.1bn in one-off items in 3Q26. NII in 3Q26 remained stable compared with 2Q26, as the benefit of the reinvestment of our structural hedge at higher yields and a higher day count were partly offset by lower NII from Markets Treasury and the impact of an adverse $0.1bn in one-off items.
 
NII in 9M26 of $27.5bn was 8% higher compared with 9M25. The increase was primarily driven by deposit balance growth, the benefit of reinvestment of our structural hedge at higher yields and the favourable impact from foreign currency translation differences of $0.4bn. This was partly offset by lower NII from Markets Treasury. The funding costs associated with generating trading and fair value income were $7.2bn, an increase of $0.1bn compared with 9M25 as the impact of higher trading balances was partly offset by lower market interest rates.
 
NIM for 3Q26 of 1.57% was stable compared with 3Q25. NIM was down 5bps in 3Q26 compared with 2Q26, driven by AIEA increasing faster than NII. NIM for 9M26 was up 3bps compared with 9M25, primarily reflecting the benefit of our structural hedge.
 
Interest income in 3Q26 of $25.9bn increased by $1.5bn or 6% compared with 2Q26, and by $1.5bn or 6% compared with 3Q25, primarily due to an increase in AIEA. On a constant currency basis, interest income rose by $1.5bn compared with 2Q26, and by $1.5bn compared with 3Q25.
 
Interest expense in 3Q26 of $16.6bn increased by $1.4bn or 10% compared with 2Q26, and by $1.0bn or 6% compared with 3Q25, primarily due to an increase in average interest-bearing liabilities. On a constant currency basis, interest expense rose by $1.5bn compared with 2Q26, and by $1.0bn compared with 3Q25.

Banking NII adjusts our NII primarily for the impact of funding trading and fair value activities reported in interest expense. It represents the Group’s banking revenue that is directly impacted by changes in interest rates. It is defined as Group net interest income after deducting:
 
-
the internal cost to fund trading and fair value net assets for which associated revenue is reported in ‘Net income from financial instruments held for trading or managed on a fair value basis’, also referred to as ‘trading and fair value income’. These funding costs reflect proxy overnight or term interest rates as applied by internal funds transfer pricing;
-
the funding cost of foreign exchange swaps in Markets Treasury, where an offsetting income or loss is recorded in trading and fair value income. These instruments are used to manage foreign currency deployment and funding in our entities; and
-
third-party net interest income in our Insurance business.
 
In our segmental disclosures, the funding costs of trading and fair value net assets are predominantly recorded in CIB in ‘net income from financial instruments held for trading or managed on a fair value basis’. On consolidation, this funding is eliminated in Corporate Centre, resulting in an increase in the funding cost reported in net interest income with an equivalent offsetting increase in ‘net income from financial instruments held for trading or managed on a fair value basis’ in this segment. In the consolidated Group results, the cost to fund these trading and fair value net assets is reported in net interest income.
 
Banking NII was $34.6bn in 9M26, an increase of $2.2bn or 7% compared with 9M25, primarily driven by deposit balance growth, the benefit of reinvestment of our structural hedge at higher yields and the favourable impact of foreign currency translation differences of $0.5bn.
 
This was partly offset by lower NII from Markets Treasury. Insurance NII, which is deducted from banking NII, reduced by $0.2bn, due to the impact of strategic transactions. The funding costs associated with generating trading and fair value income were $7.2bn, an increase of $0.1bn compared with 9M25, as the impact of higher trading balances was partly offset by lower market interest rates.
 
The internally allocated funding to generate trading and fair value income was $272bn at 30 September 2026, a rise of approximately $35bn since 30 September 2025. This related to trading, fair value and associated net asset balances, predominantly in CIB.

Balance sheet commentary – 30 September 2026 compared with 30 June 2026
 
At 30 September 2026, our total assets of $3.4tn were stable on both a reported and constant currency basis. Lending growth, net of the classification to assets held for sale of loans from the exit of our retail banking business in Australia, and growth in derivative asset balances, were broadly offset by lower trading assets and reverse repo balances.
 
Loans and advances to customers as a percentage of customer accounts were 56.1%, compared with 55.9% at 30 June 2026.
 
Loans and advances to customers of $1.0tn were $7.8bn higher on a reported basis. This included a favourable effect of foreign currency translation differences of $1.1bn. On a constant currency basis, customer lending balances increased by $6.7bn.
 
The following movements are on a constant currency basis.
 
In our UK business, customer lending rose by $7.2bn, primarily driven by continued growth in commercial lending and mortgage balances.
 
In our Hong Kong business, customer lending increased by $6.7bn, which included higher retail lending balances and the accounting reclassification of certain Wealth-related lending balances.
 
In our CIB business, customer lending increased by $4.4bn, primarily reflecting growth in Asia.
 
In our IWPB business, customer lending decreased by $11.7bn, reflecting the classification to held for sale of loans from the exit of our retail banking business in Australia. This was partly offset by lending growth as we supported our customers to participate in the India Foreign Currency Non-Resident Deposit scheme.
 
Customer accounts of $1.8tn increased by $9.1bn on a reported basis. This included the favourable effects of foreign currency translation differences of $2.6bn. On a constant currency basis, customer accounts increased by $6.5bn.
 
The following movements are on a constant currency basis.
 
In our Hong Kong business, customer accounts increased by $20.6bn reflecting continued momentum in deposit inflows, mainly into term deposits.
 
In IWPB, customer accounts increased by $9.8bn reflecting deposit growth in India as we facilitated customer participation in the India Foreign Currency Non-Resident Deposit scheme. This growth was partly offset by retail deposit outflows following our announced exit of our retail banking business in Australia.
 
In CIB, customer accounts decreased by $24.2bn, which included expected outflows of balances placed by clients for a short-term duration in both Securities Services and GPS.
 
In our UK business, customer accounts were stable despite growing competition for retail deposits.
 
Financial investments
As part of our interest rate hedging strategy and liquidity management we hold a portfolio of debt instruments, reported within financial investments, which are classified as hold-to-collect-and-sell. As a result, the change in value of these instruments is recognised through ‘debt instruments at fair value through other comprehensive income’ in equity. At 3Q26, we recognised a pre-tax cumulative unrealised loss reserve through other comprehensive income of $5.0bn related to these hold-to-collect-and-sell positions, excluding investments held in our Insurance business. This compared with an unrealised loss of $2.4bn at 2Q26, and reflected a $2.6bn pre-tax loss in 3Q26, inclusive of movements on related fair value hedges.
 
We also hold a portfolio of financial investments measured at amortised cost, which are classified as hold-to-collect. At 3Q26, the debt instruments within this portfolio had a cumulative unrecognised loss of $7.0bn, representing a $4.9bn deterioration during 3Q26.
 
Risk-weighted assets 
RWAs of $922.4bn increased by $16.0bn compared with 30 June 2026, primarily due to asset size movements of $18.7bn, driven primarily by IWPB due to increases in sovereign exposures arising from participation in the Foreign Currency Non-Resident Deposit scheme in India, lending in our CIB and UK businesses and financial commitments in our Hong Kong business. A further increase of $5.9bn reflected the impact of a redeveloped probability of default (‘PD‘) model for large corporates mainly in CIB, partly offset by reductions in our UK and Hong Kong businesses, as well as an increase for the small and medium-sized enterprises PD model in our UK business. Methodology and policy changes reduced RWAs by $6.0bn, mainly driven by a significant risk transfer transaction executed through the issuance of a credit-linked note (‘CLN‘) in our UK business, and changes to the market risk capital multiplier in CIB.
 
←  
For further details on RWAs, see page 53.
 
Business disposals
 
We reported balances of $45.5bn in assets held for sale and $23.8bn in liabilities held for sale at 30 September 2026, which were predominantly business disposal groups that met the held for sale criteria. This included a reclassification made in the third quarter of 2026 of $25.6bn in assets and $1.2bn in liabilities in respect of our retail banking business in Australia.
 
During the nine months ended 30 September 2026, we recognised net pre-tax losses of $0.8bn relating to business disposals, including $0.2bn in disposals losses and related restructuring costs and write-downs recognised in the third quarter of 2026 relating to our retail banking business in Australia. Impacts in prior quarters of 2026 included a $0.3bn disposal loss on the classification of our business in Malta as held for sale and a $0.2bn loss on the recycling of foreign currency translation reserves on completion of the sale of our UK life insurance business.
 
Australia retail banking business
On 31 July 2026, HSBC Bank Australia Limited (‘HSBC Australia’), an indirect wholly-owned subsidiary of HSBC Holdings plc, entered into an agreement to sell its portfolio of home and personal loans to Virgo BidCo Pty Ltd, an entity wholly owned by funds managed by affiliates of Blackstone Inc. The transaction has received competition approval, remains subject to regulatory approval and is expected to complete in the first half of 2027. The remainder of HSBC Australia’s retail business will be wound down in a phased manner over 18 months. Following this, HSBC Australia’s Corporate and Institutional Banking, Asset Management and Private Banking businesses in Australia will be consolidated into The Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation Limited Sydney Branch, simplifying HSBC’s entity footprint. HSBC expects to incur $0.3 bn in associated restructuring costs. Following the disposal and associated wind-down actions, we expect then to recycle foreign currency translation reserve losses to the income statement. These stood at $0.2bn at 30 September 2026. During the third quarter of 2026, we recognised a $0.2bn loss including an immaterial disposal loss and related restructuring costs and write-offs.
 
On 21 August 2026, HSBC Australia entered into a binding agreement to sell its credit card balances to Credit Corp Group Limited, on which we recognised an immaterial loss on disposal during the third quarter of 2026.
 
The home and personal loan portfolio and credit card balances met the criteria for classification as held for sale in the third quarter of 2026, with aggregate assets of $25.6bn and liabilities of $1.2bn classified as held for sale at 30 September 2026.
 
Other transactions
On 9 October 2026, HSBC Continental Europe, a wholly-owned subsidiary of HSBC Bank plc, completed the sale of its fund administration business, Internationale Kapitalanlagegesellschaft mbH, to BlackFin Capital Partners S.A.S. On completion, the associated financial impacts were immaterial.
 
On 2 August 2026, HSBC Bank Egypt S.A.E., an indirect subsidiary of HSBC Holdings plc, entered into a binding agreement to sell its retail banking business to Emirates NBD Egypt (S.A.E), a direct subsidiary of Emirates NBD Bank PJSC. The transaction remains subject to regulatory approval and is expected to complete in the second half of 2027. The disposal group did not meet the held for sale criteria in the third quarter of 2026, given a completed migration was anticipated to require more than 12 months from the reporting date. The sale is expected to generate an estimated pre-tax gain of $0.3bn, inclusive of related transaction and migration costs and write-offs, that will be recognised largely upon completion
.
On 24 July 2026, HSBC Insurance (Asia Pacific) Holdings Limited, an indirect wholly-owned subsidiary of HSBC Holdings plc, entered into an agreement to sell its Singapore insurance business, HSBC Life (Singapore) Pte. Ltd, to Allianz Asia Holdings Pte. Ltd. The disposal group met the held for sale criteria in the second quarter of 2026, with balances remaining classified as held for sale at 30 September 2026 of $10.8bn in assets and $10.5bn in liabilities, including insurance manufacturing contractual service margin of $1.4bn. The transaction, which remains subject to regulatory approval, is expected to generate an estimated pre-tax gain of $1.8bn, net of migration costs. The estimated pre-tax profit on the sale will be recognised through a combination of the consolidation of HSBC Life (Singapore) Pte. Ltd’s results into the Group’s financial statements (between the 31 December 2025 net asset reference date and until completion), and the remaining gain on sale recognised at completion, expected in the first half of 2027.
 
On 10 July 2026, HSBC Latin America Holdings (UK) Limited completed the sale of HSBC Bank (Uruguay) S.A. to a subsidiary of BTG Pactual Holding SA. On completion, we recycled immaterial foreign currency translation and other reserves losses to the income statement.
 
On 4 May 2026, PT Bank HSBC Indonesia, an indirect subsidiary of HSBC Holdings plc, entered into a binding agreement to sell its retail banking business to PT Bank OCBC NISP Tbk. The disposal group met the held for sale criteria in the second quarter of 2026, with balances remaining classified as held for sale at 30 September 2026 of $0.3bn in assets and $2.0bn in liabilities. The transaction, which is subject to regulatory approval, is expected to complete in the first half of 2027, at which point, subject to variable consideration terms, an estimated pre-tax gain of up to $0.4bn will be recognised.
 
On 30 April 2026, The Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation Limited completed the sale of its retail banking business in Sri Lanka to Nations Trust Bank PLC. An immaterial pre-tax gain on disposal was recognised following completion.
 
On 27 February 2026, HSBC Bank plc completed the transfer of its business in South Africa to local lender FirstRand Bank Ltd. Upon subsequent substantive wind-down of the entity, expected in the fourth quarter of 2026, cumulative foreign currency translation reserves and other reserves will recycle to the income statement. At 30 September 2026, foreign currency translation reserve and other reserve losses stood at $0.1bn.
 
On 30 January 2026, HSBC Bank plc completed the sale of its UK life insurance entity, HSBC Life (UK) Limited, to Chesnara plc. On completion, we recognised a loss of $0.2bn following the recycling of foreign currency translation reserves to the income statement.
 
On 22 December 2025, in line with the put option agreement entered into with CrediaBank S.A. in September 2025 and following the completion of the employee information and consultation process in France, HSBC Continental Europe signed a sale and purchase agreement for the sale of its 70.03% majority stake in HSBC Bank Malta p.l.c. The disposal group met the criteria for classification as held for sale in the first quarter of 2026, at which point a pre-tax loss on disposal of $0.3bn was recognised. As at 30 September 2026, $8.3bn of assets and $8.2bn of liabilities remained classified as held for sale. The transaction remains subject to regulatory approval and is expected to complete in the first half of 2027.
 
On 27 June 2025, HSBC Continental Europe reached an agreement to sell its custody business in Germany to BNP Paribas. The transaction is being completed in a phased manner, with a number of phases completed during 2026. While client consent and related operational requirements may extend the timing for completion of all client transfers, given the signing of a sale and purchase agreement, the disposal group met the held for sale criteria in the second quarter of 2025, with balances remaining classified as held for sale at 30 September 2026 of $0.1bn in assets and $1.9bn in liabilities. The sale is expected to generate an estimated pre-tax gain on disposal of $0.1bn, which will be recognised in line with completion of client transfers.
 
Events after the balance sheet date
On 9 October 2026, HSBC Continental Europe, a wholly-owned subsidiary of HSBC Bank plc, completed the sale of its fund administration business, Internationale Kapitalanlagegesellschaft mbH, to BlackFin Capital Partners S.A.S. On completion, the associated financial impacts were immaterial.
 
Business segments
Our business segments – Hong Kong, UK, Corporate and Institutional Banking and International Wealth and Premier Banking – along with Corporate Centre – are our reportable segments under IFRS 8 ‘Operating Segments’.
 
The Group Operating Committee is considered the Chief Operating Decision Maker (‘CODM’) for the purposes of identifying the Group’s reportable segments. Business segment results are assessed by the CODM on the basis of constant currency performance. We separately disclose ‘notable items’, as described on page 5.
 
Our operations are closely integrated and, accordingly, the presentation of data includes internal allocations of certain items of income and expense. These allocations include the costs of certain support services and global infrastructures to the extent that they can be meaningfully attributed to business segments. While such allocations have been made on a systematic and consistent basis, they necessarily involve a degree of subjectivity. Costs that are not allocated to business segments are included in Corporate Centre.
 
Where relevant, income and expense amounts presented include the results of inter-segment funding along with inter-company and inter-business line transactions. All such transactions are undertaken on arm‘s length terms. The intra-Group elimination items for business segments are presented in Corporate Centre.
 
As required by IFRS 8, reconciliations of the constant currency results to the Group’s reported results are presented on page 25. Supplementary reconciliations of constant currency to reported results by business segment are presented on pages 28 to 30 for information purposes.
 
Effective 1 January 2026, we transferred certain clients, primarily in Hong Kong and the UK, to the CIB segment to better meet their needs. This transfer does not change the Group’s reportable segments. Comparative periods have been re-presented accordingly. The re-presentation has no impact on the Group’s consolidated financial results or financial position.

Profit before tax of $7.7bn increased by $0.8bn or 12% compared with 9M25 on a constant currency basis.
 
Revenue of $12.2bn was $0.7bn or 6% higher on a constant currency basis.
 
Banking NII of $9.1bn increased by $0.5bn or 5%. The increase was mainly due to the impact of deposit balance growth and higher lending balances, partly offset by the impact of lower average margins on time deposits due to market competition, and an adverse one-off impact of $0.1bn in 9M26.
 
Fee and other income of $3.2bn was up by $0.2bn or 8%. In Retail Banking and Wealth, fee and other income increased, primarily driven by growth in Wealth, underpinned by a strong performance in Investment Distribution reflecting higher customer activity and invested asset balance growth.
 
ECL of $0.8bn in 9M26 were $0.4bn lower than in 9M25 on a constant currency basis, primarily reflecting lower charges related to the Hong Kong CRE sector.
 
Operating expenses increased by $0.2bn to $3.7bn on a constant currency basis, driven by continued investment in our Wealth business and the impact of inflation. These increases were partly mitigated by cost reductions from our organisational simplification.

Profit before tax of $5.2bn increased by $0.4bn or 8% compared with 9M25 on a constant currency basis.
Revenue of $9.9bn was $0.5bn or 5% higher on a constant currency basis.
Banking NII of $8.6bn increased by $0.5bn or 6%, reflecting the benefit of reinvestment of our structural hedge at higher yields, and growth in lending and deposit balances.
Fee and other income of $1.3bn decreased by $30m or 2% compared with 9M25, reflecting strategic actions taken to support small businesses and Premier customers.
ECL of $0.7bn in 9M26 increased by $0.1bn compared with 9M25 on a constant currency basis. The 9M26 period included the addition of allowances to reflect the ongoing uncertainty of impacts related to the conflict in the Middle East.
Operating expenses of $4.1bn were broadly stable on a constant currency basis. Increases from continued investment in technology, the impact of inflation and higher branch security costs were partly mitigated by cost reductions from our organisational simplification.

Profit before tax of $10.9bn was $1.4bn or 14% higher than in 9M25 on a constant currency basis, including a favourable impact of $0.2bn from strategic transactions, mainly notable items.
 
Revenue of $23.2bn was $1.5bn or 7% higher on a constant currency basis.
 
Banking NII of $12.0bn increased by $0.7bn or 6%, driven by balance growth across Securities Services, GPS and GTS, reflecting strong customer demand. Banking NII also rose from increased funding deployed into trading activities on higher bullion balances, as well as from strong financing demand. This was partly offset by lower Wholesale Credit and Lending banking NII, due to reduced balances and the impact of lower market interest rates across our main legal entities in Europe and Mexico compared with 9M25.
 
Fee and other income of $11.2bn increased by $0.7bn or 7%.
 
–
In WTB, fee and other income increased by $0.5bn or 7%, primarily reflecting growth in Global Foreign Exchange, an increase in volumes and new mandates across Securities Services, GPS and GTS. There was also a one-off recovery fee in GTS.
–
In Debt and Equity Markets, fee and other income increased by $0.3bn or 17%, reflecting higher Equity Derivatives, and Prime Finance income driven by increased volumes and wider margins, which were partly offset by higher funding costs on increased bullion balances.
–
In Investment Banking, fee and other income of $0.8bn was broadly stable as growth in financing was offset by the impact of the wind-down of M&A and ECM in the UK, Europe and the US.
–
 
ECL of $1.1bn in 9M26 increased by $0.6bn compared with 9M25 on a constant currency basis. The charge in 9M26 included a $0.5bn charge for a fraud-related, secondary, securitisation exposure with a financial sponsor in the UK, higher charges in Asia, as well as an increase in allowances to reflect uncertainty due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. In 9M25, charges included a single name Middle Eastern exposure.
 
Operating expenses of $11.2bn were $0.5bn or 5% lower than in 9M25 on a constant currency basis. The decrease reflected the year-on-year favourable impact from notable items, which in 9M25 primarily included a legal provision, costs associated with the wind-down of our M&A and ECM activities in the UK, Europe and the US, and impairments in Germany. Excluding notable items, operating expenses increased, reflecting higher planned spend and investment in technology, and the impact of inflation. This was partly offset by cost reductions from our organisational simplification.

Profit before tax of $3.7bn was $0.3bn or 9% higher than in 9M25 on a constant currency basis, including an adverse impact of $0.3bn from strategic transactions and notable items.
 
Revenue of $11.5bn was $0.3bn or 3% higher on a constant currency basis, including an adverse impact of $0.3bn from strategic transactions and notable items.
 
Banking NII of $5.3bn decreased by $0.2bn or 3% compared with 9M25, primarily due to lower interest rates, mainly in Asia, partly offset by growth in deposit balances.
 
Fee and other income of $6.4bn was up by $0.5bn or 9%, driven by Wealth due to growth across all products and in multiple markets, including Hong Kong, the Chinese mainland, Singapore and Taiwan.
 
In Wealth, fee and other income of $5.9bn was up by $0.6bn or 10% including an adverse impact of $0.3bn from strategic transactions.
 
–
Investment Distribution rose by $0.3bn or 29%, primarily due to higher sales of mutual funds and structured products, mainly in Asia.
–
Private Bank increased by $0.2bn or 15%, as increased customer activity supported by business initiatives led to strong performances in brokerage and trading, and from higher annuity fees, driven by growth in invested asset balances.
–
Insurance income increased by $0.1bn or 4%, including an adverse impact of $0.2bn from strategic transactions. The increase reflected a higher CSM release as a result of strong new business growth and the non-recurrence of 9M25 losses from onerous contracts, primarily in the Chinese mainland, largely offset by less favourable net investment returns.
 
In Other, fee and other income was $0.1bn lower compared with 9M25 primarily reflecting lower Markets Treasury allocations.
 
Notable items in 9M26 primarily related to losses of $0.2bn from the recycling of foreign currency translation reserves following the completion of the sale of our UK life insurance business.
 
ECL of $0.6bn in 9M26 were $0.1bn lower compared with 9M25 on a constant currency basis. This reflected a reduction in charges primarily in Mexico, mainly due to lower unsecured lending, while credit performance across the rest of the portfolio was stable.
 
Operating expenses of $7.2bn were $0.2bn or 2% higher than in 9M25 on a constant currency basis, primarily reflecting continued investments in Wealth, higher planned spend and investment in technology, and the impact of inflation. These increases were partly mitigated by cost reductions from our organisational simplification.

Profit before tax of $1.7bn was $3.0bn higher than in 9M25, on a constant currency basis.
 
Revenue was $0.8bn higher on a constant currency basis, primarily reflecting a $0.9bn net favourable impact from notable items.
 
In 9M26, notable items included a $0.3bn disposal loss recognised on classification to held for sale of our business in Malta. In 9M25, notable items included a $1.1bn dilution loss related to BoCom, and $0.1bn of fair value losses on ADRs received as part of the sale consideration for our business in Argentina, which were disposed of in 2Q25.
 
Banking NII in 9M26 excluded from NII the internal cost to fund trading and fair value of net assets, predominantly in CIB, of $7.2bn (9M25: $7.2bn). Banking NII was favourable by $0.2bn compared with 9M25 on a constant currency basis, primarily reflecting the impact of the disposal of our retained French portfolio of home and certain other loans in the second half of 2025.
 
Fee and other income was $0.3bn lower compared with 9M25, primarily driven by valuation losses on financial instruments and structural foreign exchange hedges, together with the non-recurrence of $0.1bn in fair value gains on non-qualifying hedges related to our retained French portfolio of home and certain other loans. This was partly offset by a one-off $0.2bn gain from a property asset disposal in 9M26.
 
Operating expenses were $1.1bn lower on a constant currency basis, primarily reflecting the non-recurrence of legal provisions in 9M25 of $1.1bn and lower restructuring and other related costs associated with our organisational simplification.
 
Share of profit from associates and joint ventures less impairment of $2.2bn increased by $1.0bn on a constant currency basis, primarily due to the non-recurrence of an impairment related to BoCom.

1 Impact of strategic transactions classified as material notable items.
2 For a description of how we derive banking NII, see page 11. Banking NII in Corporate Centre is computed by deducting the internal cost to fund trading and fair value net assets for which associated revenue is reported in ‘Net income from financial instruments held for trading or managed on a fair value basis’. Corporate Centre banking net interest expense includes funding charges on property and technology assets, and the banking NII of the French retained portfolio of home and other loans prior to disposal.
3 Revenue from Markets Treasury, HSBC Holdings net interest expense and hyperinflationary impacts are allocated out to the business segments, to align them better with their revenue and expense. The total Markets Treasury revenue component of this allocation for 3Q26 was $423m (3Q25: $606m).
 
Profit before tax of $0.5bn was $1.1bn higher compared with 3Q25 on a constant currency basis, primarily driven by the non-recurrence of legal provisions in 3Q25 of $1.1bn. Revenue decreased by $0.1bn on a constant currency basis, primarily due to lower fee and other income, reflecting valuation losses on financial instruments and structural foreign exchange hedges, partly offset by a $0.2bn favourable movement in banking NII which included the impact of the disposal of our retained French portfolio of home and certain other loans in the second half of 2025. In 3Q26, banking NII excluded from NII the internal cost to fund trading and fair value of net assets, predominantly in CIB, of $2.4bn (3Q25: $2.4bn).

Net new money
 
Net new money (‘NNM‘) represents our net customer inflows from Private Bank and Retail invested assets and Wealth deposits. It excludes foreign exchange movements and market and other movements not relating to client inflows/outflows, which are reported within ‘foreign exchange and others’ and ‘net market movements’, respectively. This metric excludes net customer inflows from Asset Management third-party distribution. From 1 January 2026, we disclose NNM as our key Wealth metric, offering greater comparability to industry peers. We no longer disclose invested assets as a key metric.

Risk
 
Managing risk
 
We maintain a proactive approach to managing our exposure to economic, financial and geopolitical risks, supported by continuous monitoring and review. Developments in these areas have historically affected, and may in the future adversely affect, HSBC’s customers, operations and overall risk profile, including financial risks.
 
Geopolitical developments, particularly the conflict in the Middle East, remain a source of uncertainty and have resulted in periodic financial market volatility, higher and more volatile oil and gas prices, and supply chain disruption. This environment is contributing to higher inflation with associated upward pressure on interest rates, while increasing the risk of a slowdown in global growth. For some countries, particularly those in the Middle East, where oil and gas output has been disrupted and travel, logistics and other sectors are affected, the impact on growth is already significant. Supply chain disruptions have materialised in some key trade corridors and could have long-lasting implications for the direction of trade, and for energy, military and economic security. We keep developments under close review with a focus on potential impacts on our Gulf operations, as well as our customers and suppliers.
 
We also continue to monitor the Russia-Ukraine war, including hybrid attacks across Europe attributed to Russia, and any indication of other potential military action or conflict elsewhere. Heightened strategic competition between the US and China, including cross-border investment restrictions, is also affecting the configuration of global supply chains, which may in turn affect the Group’s operations.
 
Sanctions and restrictions on trade and investment are continually evolving in response to geopolitical events and may adversely affect the Group, our customers and the markets in which the Group operates. These factors may result in increased legal, regulatory, reputational and market risks, and a more complex operating environment.
 
Trade and tariff policies remain a source of uncertainty for businesses and consumers. Changes to tariff rates, including sector-specific measures, could reduce capital investment and consumer spending, disrupt supply chains and dampen global trade growth. While the reconfiguration of trade and supply routes may create new opportunities for investment and growth, it could also have an adverse impact on the Group and our customers.
 
We remain subject to interest rate risk, which can affect net interest income, the fair value of our assets and liabilities, and overall financial performance. Changes in inflation expectations, energy prices, fiscal policy and geopolitical developments may increase interest rate volatility by altering market expectations for the timing and pace of interest rate changes by major central banks. As inflationary pressures have increased, major central banks have adopted a more restrictive policy stance. At the beginning of 2026, markets expected both the US Federal Reserve and the Bank of England (‘BoE’) to reduce policy rates. However, in the year to date, the US Federal Reserve has raised its interest rate once, while the BoE has left its policy rate unchanged.
 
Higher interest rates, or a prolonged period of restrictive policy, could reduce loan demand across key consumer and business segments, weaken credit quality and weigh on real estate and other asset prices. By contrast, lower interest rates, or faster than expected policy easing, could put downward pressure on net interest margins and adversely affect profitability. Interest rate uncertainty may contribute to broader market volatility, affecting funding costs, hedging effectiveness and the valuation of financial instruments.
 
Exchange rate volatility may also affect our risk exposure through mark-to-market changes in trading positions and the translation effects of currency movements.
 
Our risk profile may be influenced by fiscal policies, public deficits and levels of sovereign indebtedness. In many of our major markets, government debt has increased, reflecting higher social welfare commitments and expenditure on defence, energy security and climate transition. In the year to date, yields on long-term government debt have increased across major economies, amid concerns over fiscal outlooks and increased debt issuance. Higher sovereign borrowing costs could constrain fiscal capacity and adversely affect debt sustainability, particularly for highly indebted sovereigns. Elevated issuance and refinancing needs, together with changes in investor demand and market liquidity, could increase sovereign funding pressures. The growing role of non-bank financial institutions in holding and intermediating sovereign debt may amplify the transmission of market volatility, as leveraged positions can trigger forced sales when yields rise or funding conditions tighten, impairing liquidity across markets. Higher yields could also reduce the value of our sovereign bond holdings and increase private sector borrowing costs, as well as funding and refinancing risks for our customers and counterparties, with potentially negative implications for credit quality and market conditions.
 
More broadly, the continued growth of private equity and debt markets, and their increasing interconnectedness with banks and other financial institutions, may amplify the transmission of credit, liquidity and valuation risks across the financial system.
 
We continue to monitor investment and developments in the artificial intelligence (‘AI’) and technology sectors. While AI may improve productivity and support growth, there is a risk that the expected gains will fail to materialise or will take longer than expected. This could contribute to a disruptive correction to the valuations of AI and technology-related assets. AI adoption could also disrupt established business models and labour markets, potentially increasing unemployment in certain sectors and markets. These risks could affect HSBC’s risk profile and earnings by impairing the creditworthiness of borrowers, increasing the financial vulnerability of customers and decreasing the value of collateral and other claims.
 
In Hong Kong, real estate market conditions continued to stabilise in the third quarter of 2026. The recovery nevertheless remains uneven, with improved leasing activity in prime office and retail locations but higher vacancies, valuation pressure and subdued investor appetite continuing in non-prime segments. Sentiment in the residential property market remains resilient. The recent increase in interest rates and inflationary pressure present a headwind to the broader recovery. Further increases could weaken sentiment and trigger a softening of demand.
 
In the third quarter of 2026, management adjustments to ECL were applied to reflect sector or portfolio risks that are not fully captured by our models. We continue to monitor, and seek to manage, the potential implications of all the above developments on our customers and our business.
 
At 30 September 2026, our CET1 ratio decreased to 13.9% from 14.1% at 30 June 2026, and our liquidity coverage ratio (‘LCR’) was 132%, down from 134% at 30 June 2026.

Credit risk
 
Summary of credit risk
At 30 September 2026, gross loans and advances to banks and customers of $1,146bn increased by $38.0bn on a reported basis compared with 31 December 2025. Gross loans and advances to customers increased by $42.1bn and gross loans and advances to banks decreased by $4.1bn. This included total adverse foreign exchange movements of $6.0bn.
 
On a constant currency basis, the increase of $47.7bn in loans and advances to customers was driven by higher balances in our CIB business (up $23.1bn), our UK business (up $17.8bn) and in our Hong Kong business (up $15.3bn). These were partly offset by an $8.5bn decrease in our IWPB business.
 
The increase in CIB was driven by higher balances in our entities in Asia, the US and the Middle East across several sectors.
 
In our UK business, the increase was primarily driven by higher corporate and commercial exposures in addition to mortgage growth.
 
The increase in our Hong Kong business was primarily driven by higher balances across other personal lending and corporate and commercial exposures.
 
The decrease in IWPB was driven by the classification to held for sale of loans from the planned sale of our portfolios of home and personal loans, and credit card balances in Australia. This was partly offset by growth in our entities in India and Hong Kong.
 
At 30 September 2026, the allowance for ECL of $11.9bn increased by $0.7bn compared with 31 December 2025, including write-offs of $2.8bn and favourable foreign exchange movements of $0.1bn. The $11.9bn allowance comprised $11.5bn in respect of assets held at amortised cost and $0.4bn in respect of loan commitments and financial guarantees.
 
On a constant currency basis, the allowance for ECL in relation to loans and advances to customers increased by $0.8bn. This was attributable to:
 
–
a $0.8bn increase in allowance for ECL on wholesale loans and advances to customers, which included a $0.7bn increase in stage 3 and a $0.1bn increase in stages 1 and 2; and
–
a broadly unchanged allowance for ECL on personal loans and advances to customers across all stages.
The ECL charge for the first nine months of 2026 was $3.2bn (9M25: $2.9bn), inclusive of recoveries. It comprised: $1.1bn in respect of CIB; $0.8bn in respect of the Hong Kong business; $0.7bn in respect of the UK business; and $0.6bn in respect of IWPB.

The 9M26 charge primarily reflected a $0.5bn fraud-related, secondary, securitisation exposure with a financial sponsor in the UK in our CIB business, as well as an increase in allowances to reflect heightened uncertainty and a deterioration in the forward economic outlook due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The net ECL charge in the Hong Kong CRE sector was $0.3bn in 9M26.
